en: Homage to Śrī Vajraḍāka!
Having bowed to the Lord Śrī Heruka, who is the blissful essence of the three bodies, I shall, out of faith, write down something that has come down through the succession of the lineage of gurus. 1.
Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret in brief and not at length:
the union with Śrī Heruka, which accomplishes all desires and aims. (HA 1.1)
Even higher than the highest is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*,
which always abides within the secret, supreme, and delightful self of all.
The being consisting of all ḍākinīs is Vajrasattva, the supreme bliss;
for he is the self-arisen Blessed One, the Hero, the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. (HA 1.3)

By the words beginning with "atha" (now), this tantra is shown to be connected with other tantras; therefore, this word "atha" indicates the immediate succession of this tantra in relation to the preceding tantra. Since it was stated in the *Trilakṣābhidhāna* that [the teaching] was spoken by "Evam mayā" (Thus by me), for that very reason, the introductory statement of the causal origin (*nidānavākya*) has not been employed at the beginning of this [tantra], because it has already been employed previously. 2.

*Tantra* means a continuous sequence (*prabandha*). It consists of the causal *tantra*, the resultant *tantra*, and the method *tantra*. Among these, the cause is the spiritual lineage (*gotra*). In this very context, practitioners are even more difficult to find. The method *tantra* refers to the practices such as meditation, recitation, offerings, mantras, and ritual diagrams, following the sequence beginning with entry into the maṇḍala preceded by the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*). The result is non-duality, which culminates solely in luminosity, is beyond the sphere of speech, and is far removed from the fluctuations of the mind. How, then, can that be a continuous sequence?

The meaning is that by means of this, the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma) abide here. Its seal (mudrā) is the syllable A; the meaning is that, through its conventional form, sounds and phonemes originate from it.
It is also stated in the *Śrīvajramaṇḍālaṃkāra*:
"The unstruck sound (anāhata), blazing like a lamp, situated in the center of the heart."
"The supreme syllable is the most subtle; the letter A is the supreme Lord.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Dvikalparāja*:
"The Mahāmudrā resides at the navel, her hand holding a blazing lamp-flame."
That wisdom (*dhī*) has been conceived by the Buddhas as having the nature of the primordial vowel (*ādi-svara*).

From this [vowel] "a," everything will be explained; such is the connection. What is that? It is the secret (*rahasya*). It is not to be revealed to those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*). What is it that is not to be revealed? That which is to be hidden consists of seven things, namely:

the secret teaching on reality (*tattva*), the secret five seed-syllables (*bījapañcaka*), [the secret of the mandala, the secret of the mudrās, the secret of the mantras, the secret of the deities, and the secret of the ritual].
In the secret, which is the hidden true nature; in the secret, the hidden lotus.
In the secret [teaching] of Vijayānanda, in the secret [teaching] of Sarvasaṃgama, and in the secret [teaching] of Sukhānantarya—thus [it is said]. ||8||

"From the compendium" (*samāsāt*) means by way of brevity in terms of the extent of the text, but not in terms of its meaning, because it encompasses all the qualities of a Buddha (*sarvabuddhadharma*). For this very reason, it is called "the compendium" (*saṃvara*); the meaning is that it restrains (*saṃvṛṇoti*) and grasps (*gṛhṇāti*) everything.

(9) "The union with Śrī Heruka" refers to Śrī Heruka as one's own self. The *mudrā* is Vajravārāhī. The union of these two is characterized as the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). (10) Desires are those things which are desired; they are the fulfillment of wished-for aims. Because one accomplishes the state of all Buddhas and the state of the Vajra-holder by means of this very [union], it is "the accomplisher of all desires and aims" (*sarvakāmārthasādhaka*). (11)

What is that? It is "even higher than the high. "The high" has its meaning already explained. By virtue of the diversity of the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings with various interests, there is the teaching of eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) for the sake of purifying the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Even higher than that is the "unsurpassed," the reality residing in the heart. It is not grasped by the paths of speech by any Buddhas together with the Vajra-holders, because it exists as a form to be personally realized within each individual. Therefore—

"Those devoid of reality do not achieve success even in hundreds of millions of eons," thus it was said by the Blessed One. (13) Regarding the title *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, he describes the excellence of the assembly. The root *ḍai* means "to move through the air. The vowel *ai* becomes *ā*. *Ḍānaṃ* is *ḍāḥ*; the meaning is "moving through space. From the word *ḍā*, the third case suffix is applied. The root *ak* means "to go crookedly"; here, moving everywhere constitutes the crooked movement. She whose nature (*śīla*) is to *akitum* (go) with *ḍā* is a *ḍākinī*. The meaning is that she moves simultaneously in all directions by means of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodies. *Jāla* means their collection or multitude.
The *śaṃvara* is the supreme bliss, because [the practitioner] is satisfied moment by moment with them.
(14) By the words "in secret" (*rahasye*) and so forth, the void consisting of sixteen syllables is indicated. By the word "all" (*sarva*), these are spoken of:
(15) "By the letter *ra* is the blood-element, and by the letter *ha* is the 'born of the mountain' (*girija*). Here, "born of the mountain" refers to the hair of the head (*śiroja*).
The letter *sy* is the vessel for fragrance; as there is fragrance in the body, the letter *pa* is taught to be speed. (16)
By the syllable *ra*, fragrance is indeed declared; by the syllable *me*, flower is intended.
Likewise, by the syllable *ra*, salt is [intended]; by the syllable *mye*, meat is intended. ||17||

In the syllable *sa*, there is *kundura*; in the syllable *rva*, the head is said to be located; in the syllable *tma*, O Goddess, there is *nalaja*; and in the syllable *ni*, there is *gandhataila*. (18)

The syllable *sa* is considered to be sandalwood (*daṃśakara*), the syllable *dā* is from the ocean-born (*sāgaraja*), the syllable *sthi* is the essence of the crane (*sārasāra*), and the syllable *taḥ* is camphor (*karpūra*). ||19||

Alternatively—the letter E is omniscient, all-pervading, subtle, equal to the heart, the secret place, and so forth; she is the form of *māyā*, empty, the very nature of the mind, yet non-mind; like a wish-fulfilling gem, she is of an unsurpassed essence and is known as Wisdom (*prajñā*). She is remembered as the Secret and is renowned as such. (20) By ultimate meaning, she is the supreme *dharmakāya*.
(21) She is called the delightful *vipaśyanā* of omniscient knowledge. She is the lamp of innate bliss, by virtue of the nature of all things which are inconceivable, stable, and immovable. (22)
Regarding "in its universal nature": consciousness and mind, which are all the sense-faculties, exist everywhere and in every way.
What is known as mental cognition is designated as wisdom (*prajñā*), intelligence (*buddhi*), and mindfulness (*mati*). (23)

"Always" (*sadaiva*) refers to that which consists of the past, future, and present; by this, it is stated that [the Buddha] is devoid of arising and destruction, is all-pervasive, possesses a vajra-body, holds authority, is eternally manifest, and is eternal.
(24) "Abiding" (*sthita*) means: everywhere, in every realm, among all sentient beings, and in every way.
Pervading equally the entire body, it remains like the stream of consciousness. ||25||
It is untainted, inconceivable, stainless, and inherently free from the sense of "mine";
it is empty, equal to space, and devoid of both existence and non-existence. ||26||
Without beginning or end, peaceful, the embodiment of the sovereign of all phenomena, she assumes all forms while resting upon the two truths. (27)
Just as the seed of fire is established depending upon fuel, or just as oil is in sesame seeds, so too is [the embryo] established within the element. (28)
The Great Seal (mahāmudrā) is to be realized; this is the intended meaning.

[29] "The being consists of all ḍākinīs" means that by the word "all ḍākinīs," the great mothers such as Pracaṇḍā and the others are meant. Because he is composed of their atoms and because his nature is identical to theirs, he consists of them. Who is he? It is the "being" (sattva). There are two types: the stationary and the moving. As it is said: "The being is known as the moving, while the vessel and so forth are the stationary."

From this statement: "Vajrasattva is supreme bliss. *Vajra* means the indivisible; it is called *vajra* because, by virtue of its similarity to a diamond, it pierces all other things. *Sattva* is the state of being (*sadbhāva*), which is the oneness of all phenomena. Thus, that which is both *vajra* and *sattva* is Vajrasattva.
(31) "Bliss is existence, and the absence of bliss is Vajrasattva; he is remembered as bliss. (32)

Regarding the phrase "asau hi": *hi* is used for emphasis. He alone is being described: he is called *svayaṃbhū* because the entire world, including the stable and the moving, arises from himself; he is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*). He is the Blessed One because he possesses *bhaga*. By the word *bhaga*, the sixfold qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and so forth are meant.
Alternatively, it is said that *bhaga* is so called because of "breaking" (*bhañjana*), due to his breaking of the enemy of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*) and the others.
"And those afflictions are to be slain by wisdom; therefore, wisdom is called Bhaga.

(34) He is a hero because he is free from afflictions. The "net of ḍākinīs" is that which is gathered in the form of the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*); it is considered *Saṃvara*, the supreme bliss. (35) Alternatively, from the words "even more than the north," etc.: the "north" refers to the sixteen elements (*dhātu*). Even more than that are the twenty-four ḍākinīs. Their "net" is their assembly. Because they themselves are gathered in the form of the channels, they are *Saṃvara*. (36)

He states the opening of the introductory words, which are extremely secret, according to reality: "In the secret (*rahasye*)... thus (*evam*)... by me (*mayā*)... in the supreme (*parame*)... heard (*śrutam*)... in the delightful (*ramye*)... in the all-soul (*sarvātmani*). Here, the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "not through tradition. At what time? "Always situated in that which" (*sadā sthito yasmin*). Where? "In the place of great bliss" (*mahāsukhe sthāne*). Who is he? This should be construed as "that self-existent Blessed One" (*asau svayaṃbhūr bhagavān*). Alternatively: "In the secret, the element of earth; and likewise in the supreme, water."
In the delightful one known as Tejas, who is the self of all and the ever-moving wind. ||38||
"The space-element is always present" (verse 39).

That being whose all elements consist of all ḍākinīs is Vajrasattva. "Supreme" means most excellent. "Bliss" means great bliss (*mahāsukha*). The connection is that the Blessed One, being such as this, will speak [as follows] (verse 40).
Emerging from the sound-form of *saṃbhava*, they are the domain of the conduct of the pledge (*samaya*).
That which abides as the beginning, middle, and end is difficult to find within the three worlds. (HA 1.4)

Regarding the term *śambhavāt*: *śam* means bliss; its *bhava* (existence) arises because it is inferable through great passion (*mahārāga*). Therefore, "from that form of sound" means from the form of the sound of the syllable *HŪṂ* situated within the *vajramaṇi*. From that, all the heroes and yoginīs of the three times and the triple world emerge. Their *samaya* is considered to be their union (*mīlana*) through the conjunction of the *vajra* and the *padma*. *Ācāra* is the conduct (*ācaraṇa*) of the twelve sense objects and faculties. It is characterized by the consciousness that attains the range of one's own mind in the form of what is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedya*). 41.

In the beginning, within the secret [reality], there is knowledge alone—devoid of the five coverings (*pañcāvaraṇa*), pure like space, stainless in its middle and end, and perfectly established, because it is by nature pure and because delusion has been utterly destroyed. 42.
Just as [fire arises] from the union of the fire-drill and the base-wood, so too [knowledge arises] through the application of mantra-recitation, meditation, and other means.
And listen to the yoga and the knowledge of the ritual procedures as they are declared in the Tantra. HA 1.5.

"Just as the conjunction of the fire-drill, the base, and human effort [produces fire], so it is. For example: depending upon the fire-drill wood (*kāṇḍa*), the base (*manthanīya*), and the exertion of a person's hands, smoke appears and fire is produced. Yet, that fire, when sought within the fire-drill wood, the base, or the hands of the person, is not found in any one of them. Just so is this fire. The object to be churned is said to be the arising of phenomena (*dharmodaya*); the churning stick is called the *vajra*.
From their conjunction, the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*) arises, which directly brings about Buddhahood. (44)
Wisdom is the knowledge arising from the body, equal to space and endowed with its means;
through consecration, it arises perfectly as a single form, great bliss. (45)

"Listen, O Lord of Guhyakas, to that which is declared in the *tantra* as being joined with mantra-recitation, meditation, and so forth," thus spoke the Blessed One. By the word *tantra*, this entire discourse—from the words beginning with "Now" (*atha*) up to its conclusion—is intended as the summary meaning of the seal (*mudrā*). Because it protects the mind, "mantra" is wisdom (*jñāna*). Meditation (*dhyāna*) is characterized by one-pointedness of mind. Alternatively, by the word "mantra," recitation (*jāpa*) is explained as the vocalization of the *ali* and *kāli* [vowel and consonant] series.
"By means of the great exertion of the *bodhicitta*, he himself is the sovereign lord of yoga."
This bodhicitta is the vajra, because it has the nature of all buddhas. ||47||
One should always worship the Kulikā with the medium-superior breath together with scented water, according to the specific time.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the medium and superior breaths": the first, eleven years of age, is beneficial for alchemy (*rasāyana*) once she has opened her lotus; the second, twelve years of age, is for the purpose of the occasion of sexual union (*surata*); the third, sixteen years of age, possesses flowers [of menses] through the constant practice of mantra; the fourth, twenty years of age, is the best, by means of accomplishing the siddhi of moving through the sky (*khecarasiddhi*); and the fifth, twenty-five years of age, is for the purpose of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). These have been shown according to the sequence of the five knowledges through the purification of the mirror and so forth.
By "breaths" is meant that she follows the conduct together with a well-consecrated woman, headed by one's own tutelary deity. 48.

Having taken hold of a woman of noble family (*kulikā*), a maiden of noble family (*kulakanyā*), or another [woman], one should consecrate her by the depositing of the *bodhicitta*. "With perfume" (*gandha*) means having adorned her with various garments, ornaments, and so forth. "With water" (*udaka*) means all [substances] of various kinds are to be understood. Having given what is beneficial for those born of wind, bile, and phlegm in due order, and having performed worship, one should become the essence of worship. One should manifest oneself as the state of all Buddhas, illuminating the ten directions by means of the lamp of the light of gnosis (*jñānāloka*), which brings about perfect awakening through the form of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of indicating a restriction. Being intent upon the reality of meditation, one should do this constantly and without interruption. (49)

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "by means of the breath": at the time of the union of the breaths in the left and right channels at the base of the navel, that mudrā is indeed the supreme syllable (paramākṣarā). ||50||

There is an alternative reading: *madhyamottamasamāsena*. He explains that: it exists in the interval between the beginning and the end, namely childhood and old age; thus, it is the "middle passion" (*madhyamaṃ rajaḥ*). This refers to the compound *madhyamottamasamāsa*, which is characterized by a group [of terms]. Therefore, he says: "but together with scented water. Scented water is *sihlakam* (benzoin). Camphor is accompanied by that. One should worship the *kulikā* in such a manner. 51.

"By way of specific times" refers to the description of the seasonal regimen (*ṛtubandha*), because [the body] cannot avoid passion and other [afflictions] during those periods. Due to the regulation of the forenoon time, six seasons are specified: dryness, the rainy season, autumn, winter, the cool season, and the union of lovers. Having recognized the clear season, one should commence all ritual actions. (52) And it is said: "At dawn, there is the arrival of cold."
Know that the spring season is at dawn; the wise should recognize the summer as being at midday. ||53||
The rainy season [is assigned] to the afternoon, autumn likewise to the evening, and the winter to midnight. ||54||
Through the thorough knowledge of this intrinsic nature, the Victors such as Vajrasattva and the others arise. It is said:
(55) "Vajrasattva is in the cold season, the Sage Vairocana in spring; Paramāśva is indeed in the heat, and likewise Heruka in the rainy season. (56)
Vajrasūrya, however, delights in the lotus during autumn;
in winter, one should consume the lamp; likewise, in summer or the rainy season, one should consume water.
In the autumn season, indeed, [one should use] oil; likewise, flowers in the early winter;
camphor in the late winter; and likewise, the "four-identical" (catuḥsama) [ointment] in the spring.
These great medicinal herbs, infused during the six seasons, are unsurpassed among all yogic practices; there is nothing equal to the worship performed according to the seasons. (59)
When the perfection of this intrinsic nature occurs for the yogin, all the yoginīs and the assembly of yoga-ḍākinīs are satisfied. (60)
The messengers are innate, accomplished, and of low, superior, or middling [status];
one should contemplate the accomplishment of desire with an inward-turned mind.

The messengers, being thus honored, become pleased. "Inferior," and so forth, refers to what was stated previously. One should constantly meditate with an internal mind upon that which has arisen together with her, because of its nature as such. "Accomplishment of desire" means the accomplishment of Vajradhara. The word "tu" (but/and) is used for emphasis. 61. One should worship the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with the drops of one's own semen.
And by means of seeing and touching, as well as hearing and remembering. (HA 1.8)
In this very way, one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
Yogic state is supreme merit, pure, and the destroyer of evil.
The practitioner, being well-composed, achieves success by reciting the mantra through recitation and meditation, while constantly observing the commitments.
However, through the division of the *samayas*, success is not attained in the initiation mandala.
"Svaretas," "karpūra," and so forth—these should be worshipped according to the literal meaning [of the text]. 62.
Sweet-smelling, mixed with camphor and combined with red sandalwood.
Established in the midst of the assembly, bearing the marks and signs of all vajras, the knower of yoga should always lick [the substance] with the ring finger and the thumb. HA 1.12.
Having tasted it like the drinking of soma, one attains eternal perfection;
this shall become the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), which sets all accomplishments in motion. (HA 1.13)

“Madhu” means great honey. “Rakta” refers to flowers. “With camphor” (*sakarpūram*) means it exists together with camphor; this refers to the flower, not in a different sequence [of the list]. “Red sandalwood” (*raktacandana*) is flesh. “Combined” (*yojitam*) means combined with *viḍ* and the other [substances]; this is the sixth nectar, the elixir (*rasāyana*). “Marked by the vajra” (*vajrāṅkam*) means arisen from the *dharmodaya*. Alternatively, the “all-vajra” is the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka; his mark (*aṅka*), the sign, is the skull-cup (*kapāla*). Holding that in one’s own hand is what is meant by “holding there” (*tatra dhṛk*). 63.

The ring finger is the earth; the thumb is joined with Sumeru. One should churn the water with this threefold [mudrā] and make it known as being like the nectar of milk and water. (64) Regarding food, one should make it known with:
Oṃ ha ho hrīḥ.
The syllable *ha* is the destroyer of color, and *ho* is the destroyer of scent;
through the syllable *hrīḥ*—[uttered as] "blaze! blaze!"—the body is perfected.

The wise should lick the perfected nectar (*siddhāmṛta*). Having first given it to the Guru, and thereafter to the Vajrin named Heruka, one should give the mudrā and then lick it oneself. This is the essence of the five nectars, produced through union. By means of this yoga, one becomes equal to the Holder of the Vajra. 66.

Alternatively, "with camphor" means with the *bodhicitta*. "Established in the midst of the assembly" refers to the entire group of sense faculties, such as the eyes and so forth; the number of the assembly is sevenfold, including both types of faculties, and [the substance] is joined within them. What is that pair? It begins with "by means of the mouths of the ring finger and the thumb. The ring finger is the lotus (*padma*), and the thumb is the vajra. By their two mouths—that is, by means of those two, the mouths of the ring finger and the thumb—one should lick, which means one should taste it. (67)
The fourfold worship, as well as the yoginīs, and the Holder of Reality (tattvadhṛk) who has entered into the non-dual union with the Hero. HA 1.14.

The fourfold worship and likewise the yoginīs constitute the fourfold vajra. Namely: (68) first, the awakening to emptiness; second, the withdrawal of the seed-syllable; third, the accomplishment of the image; and fourth, the placement of the syllables. (69)
Above the *kalaśa* is the skull-cup (*kapāla*), and likewise the four *yoginīs*, beginning with *Ḍākinī*. By this, the meaning is that the one whose self is the maṇḍala-circle performs the worship.

(70) For this very reason, he who maintains the reality (*tattvadhṛk*) has entered into the union of non-duality with the Hero (*vīra*). "Hero" refers here to the union of practice together with the twenty-four [deities]. In this context, Kākāsyā and the others are the purifications of faith and so forth. By the word "hero," there is an inclusion of all [the deities], just as when "the king" is mentioned, it is said that there is an inclusion of everyone. (71)

Having understood this distinction, those who practice the stages of generating the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) should perform the rites for the ḍākinīs and other goddesses during the four junctions (saṃdhyā), since they are of the nature of the four liberations (vimokṣa). The non-dual worship with the heroes through meditative union (samāpatti) should also be performed. 72.

Furthermore, regarding what one who practices the stage of completion (*pariniṣpannakrama*) does while abiding in the ego-sense that is without beginning or end—since there is no restriction of time—it is said: One should meditatively cultivate (*bhāvayet*) the state of the all-pervading Great Vajradhara, who is endowed with union through entering into the consort (*mudrā*) in the proper manner; who is established in all space; who is Samantabhadra, the universal self; who is the awakening of the Buddhas; and who is the triple realm, remaining in silence.

Just as when the sun has reached the meridian, it does not differentiate between inferior, middling, or superior objects but illuminates them all around, so too, when the yogin’s knowledge of universal investigation transcends the stages of all non-Buddhist sectarians, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas and becomes free from appearances (nirābhāsa), then—by means of the rays of the Buddha-sun—it illuminates all the Tathāgatas, their teachings, and the triple world in all the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions; it does not conceptualize nor differentiate, but knows things as they truly are (yathābhūtam).
This is the meaning of "one who upholds reality" (tattvadhṛk). 73.
Even if the happiness of both divine and human states were condensed into a single diamond atom, it would not equal even a sixteenth part [of this]. (HA 1.15)

What [fraction] (*kalā*) is it compared to human existence (*mānuṣya*)? Having understood that the happiness of being human is thus condensed into a single mass, one wishes to weigh it against another yoga by means of this "diamond-atom" (*vajrakaṇikā*). Then, the phrase "they do not equal even a sixteenth part" (*kalāṃ nārghanti ṣoḍaśīm*) is merely an illustration; it does not admit of even a fraction (*kalā*), a calculation (*gaṇanā*), a comparison (*upamā*), or a likeness (*aupamya*). 74.
In mountain caves or groves, or on the shores of the great ocean, or in a cremation ground where the primordial siddhas dwell— one should there draw the mandala.
Now he speaks of the perfection of the location, beginning with "on a mountain" (girau) and so forth. It is easy to understand according to the literal meaning. 75.

He says that "the mountain" (*girih*) is specifically the secret place because there are qualities in the great lotus of the Buddha-seal through the *mlecchita* [sounds]. By implication, this means his dwelling in a secluded region of dense forest. Here, by mentioning the principal, the retinue is also included. The "dense forest of afflictions" refers to the woman-seal (*strīmudrā*), consisting of passion and other defilements; through the purification of skillful means, she herself becomes the path to enlightenment, as one reaches the ultimate limit of her purification. The "region" is called the *dharmodayā*.

That very place is secluded (*vijana*) because it arises from the birth of distinguished maidens belonging to the Vajra family and others praised by all the Tathāgatas. It is a mountain (*giri*) because its nature is immovable great bliss (*acalamahāsukha*), and because it cannot be shaken by the winds arising from false doctrines. It is a thicket (*gahvara*) because it is impossible for beings of little merit to fathom. It is a bower (*kuñja*) because it is filled with the nectar of the Victors (*jināmṛta*). "On the shores of the great ocean" means on the shores of the ocean of the profound and vast wisdom that is the union of method and insight (*prajñopāya*).

"Primordially accomplished" (*ādisiddha*) means eternally accomplished; it is the ultimate perfection, devoid of rising and setting, always equal to space. It is a "charnel ground" (*śmaśāna*) because it is burned by the fires of passion of the Śrāvakas and other Buddhas. Alternatively, because of its equality, it is the charnel ground that dwells within the mental continuums (*saṃtāna*) of all sentient beings. "Therein" means in such a distinguished place. "Maṇḍala" is so called because it takes (*lāti*) or grasps (*gṛhṇāti*) the essence (*maṇḍa*). "One should draw" means one should meditate with the mind. The external [explanation] is easy to understand. (76) The maṇḍala is the supreme reality, the highest wisdom of Śrī Heruka.
The mandala is the lotus of the bhaga, arising from the body of Vārāhī. ||77||
The mandala is the union; therein, the mandala is supreme bliss.
The mandala is indeed the non-dual union of the hero and the yoginī. (78)
The meditative absorption on the reality of the self, the reality of the deity, the reality of the mantra, and the mudrā—this is the supreme maṇḍala. ||79||
Transcending the cultivation of all limbs, free from conceptual construction and its alternatives, and beyond measure and the drop—this is the supreme maṇḍala. ||80||
The investigation of all phenomena, the discernment of what is dharma and what is non-dharma—this is declared to be the mandala, pure and resembling the sky. (81)
The womb, equal in its passion and dispassion, resembling the brilliance of a ruby, with a mind colored by divine passion—this is the supreme maṇḍala. //82//
This stainless one, which enters into all beings among both the formed and the formless, and which awakens and impels the mind—this is called the mandala. //83//
The body is said to be the maṇḍala, and the bhaga is also the maṇḍala;
the bodhicitta is likewise the maṇḍala—thus is the conceptualization of the three maṇḍalas. (84)
"Thus, the mandala is omniscient, comprising the earth, the atmosphere, and all that is moving and unmoving.
Thus ends the commentary on the first chapter of the *Pañjikā* (Explanatory Commentary) on the *Sādhananidhi*, titled the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
